name: pdf
title: Merge or split PDFs with a script
pitch: The same useful job as the Python PDF project, done with command-line tools and a bash script. You learn to glue existing programs together, which is what the shell is best at.

steps.do: Create a test folder and COPY a few PDFs into it.
steps.done: the folder holds 2 or 3 PDFs, and the originals are safe somewhere else.
steps.hint: `mkdir` and `cp`. Put one file with a space in its name, like "my scan.pdf": you'll need it later.
steps.why: Scripts act fast and don't ask twice. Practising on copies means a mistake costs nothing.

steps.do: Install the tools with your package manager: poppler-utils and qpdf.
steps.hint: `sudo apt install poppler-utils qpdf` on Debian and Ubuntu, `sudo dnf install poppler-utils qpdf` on Fedora and Rocky.
steps.why: In the shell, you rarely write the hard part yourself: you find the right tool and combine it with others. Packages are how you get them.

steps.do: Print how many pages a PDF has with pdfinfo.
steps.done: the number matches what your PDF reader shows.
steps.hint: `pdfinfo file.pdf` prints many lines; `grep` keeps the one you want, and `awk` can keep only the number.
steps.why: Many tools print more than you need. Cutting their output down to one value is a skill you'll use in every script.

steps.done: merged.pdf has the pages of both, in order.
steps.hint: `pdfunite a.pdf b.pdf merged.pdf`: the last name is the output. With qpdf: `qpdf --empty --pages a.pdf b.pdf -- merged.pdf`.
steps.why: Read the order of arguments carefully: with pdfunite, the last one is the file it writes. Getting it wrong overwrites one of your PDFs, which is why you work on copies.

steps.do: Merge every PDF in the folder, sorted by name, including files with spaces in their names.
steps.done: one file holds all of them, and "my scan.pdf" is included.
steps.hint: A glob like `*.pdf` is already sorted. Quote it right: `"$@"` or an array keep names with spaces whole.
steps.why: Spaces in file names break more shell scripts than anything else. Quoting variables every time is the habit that prevents it.

steps.do: Extract one page, then a range of pages (2 to 4), into a new PDF.
steps.done: each new file has exactly the pages you asked for.
steps.hint: `qpdf in.pdf --pages . 2-4 -- out.pdf`, or pdfseparate then pdfunite.
steps.why: Different tools, same job: knowing two ways to do something helps when one of them isn't installed.

steps.do: Split a whole PDF into one file per page.
steps.hint: `pdfseparate in.pdf page-%d.pdf`: the %d becomes the page number.
steps.why: Some tools take a pattern for their output names. Reading a tool's manual (`man pdfseparate`) often saves you writing a loop.

steps.do: Put it all in a script pdf.sh that takes the action first: `./pdf.sh merge out.pdf a.pdf b.pdf` and `./pdf.sh split a.pdf`.
steps.done: both actions work without editing the script.
steps.hint: Start with `#!/usr/bin/env bash`, `chmod +x`. `$1` is the action; `shift` removes it, then `"$@"` is the rest. A `case` picks the action.
steps.why: A script with arguments is a new command of your own. `case` is the shell's way to choose between several actions, and it reads clearly.

steps.do: Handle mistakes: a missing file, a file that isn't a PDF, an output file that already exists, and a command that fails.
steps.done: each mistake prints a clear message, and the script exits with a code that isn't 0.
steps.hint: `set -euo pipefail` at the top, `[[ -e $file ]]` to test, `file --mime-type` to check it's a PDF, and `exit 1` after the message (sent to stderr with `>&2`).
steps.why: Exit codes are how scripts tell other programs they failed. Messages go to stderr so they never end up mixed with real output.

steps.do: Optional: rotate pages, or add a `--help` message.
steps.done: it works on one test file.
steps.hint: qpdf has `--rotate`. A help message is a `case` branch that prints how to use the script.
steps.why: A help message is the first thing a stranger reads. Writing one makes you see your tool through their eyes.
